justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assess as a current baseline price in the low-to-mid 360s range. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 362.5 is essentially anchored to recent price levels with very little directional conviction, as short-term price movements in most financial assets are nearly impossible to predict with meaningful edge. The one-week estimate of 364 and one-month estimate of 367 incorporate a slight positive drift assumption, consistent with the long-run tendency of equity markets or similar assets to drift upward over time, though the increment is deliberately small to avoid overconfidence in any directional view.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect empirically observed volatility at each time horizon. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus 7.5 points reflects typical daily price fluctuation ranges. The one-week interval widens to a 30-point range, scaling approximately with the square root of time as volatility theory suggests. The one-month interval widens further to about 58 points, capturing the compounding uncertainty over a longer period. These widths assume relatively normal market conditions without major structural breaks.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock such as an unexpected inflation reading, a central bank policy surprise, or a geopolitical escalation could compress risk appetite sharply and drive prices below the lower bounds. A credit event or liquidity crisis could produce even more severe dislocations. On the upside, a strongly positive surprise in economic data, an unexpected dovish pivot by a major central bank, or a significant positive earnings catalyst could push prices above the upper bounds of my intervals.

It's also worth noting that my intervals, while wide by everyday standards, are still finite and will be violated some percentage of the time by construction. Fat-tailed events, sometimes called black swans, occur more frequently in financial markets than a normal distribution would imply. Liquidity crises, flash crashes, or geopolitical shocks can produce moves that dwarf even a well-calibrated 90% confidence interval, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is simply more time for unexpected events to accumulate.
